does: Breaks hard or firm food down to a powder, a coarse meal or a paste, by crushing it in a mortar, milling it in a grinder or running it through a blade, so that it blends into a dish or binds into a dough.

intro.what: Grinding breaks firm food into a powder, meal or paste suited to the dish.
intro.why: It teaches you to control batch size, heat and added liquid so the texture stays even.
intro.idea: Match the grind to the dish

how: Dry whole spices lightly in a warm pan first, so that they grind finer and smell stronger, then let them cool.
Soak dried pulses and drain them well before grinding them, and cut meat into strips and chill it first.
Grind in short bursts or with steady circles, a small amount at a time, so that the heat of the blade does not cook the food.
For a paste, add a very little liquid, a spoonful at a time, to keep the blades turning.
Stop when it has the texture the dish asks for, and scrape down the sides once.

cues.text: The food falls into an even powder or paste with no whole pieces left.
Spices turn sharply fragrant as they break.
A ground paste holds together when pressed between the fingers.

mistakes.mistake: Grinding a large amount at once, so that some is dust and some is whole.
mistakes.fix: Grind a little at a time.

mistakes.mistake: Running a machine for long, so that the heat dulls the scent or cooks the food.
mistakes.fix: Work in short bursts and let it rest.

mistakes.mistake: Adding too much liquid to a paste, which turns it to soup.
mistakes.fix: Add a spoonful at a time and stop as soon as it turns.

quiz.question: What determines when to stop grinding?
choices: The longest time the machine can run.
A completely smooth result for every food.
The powder, meal or paste texture the dish needs.
quiz.because: Grinding can produce different textures; stop at the texture needed rather than always making a smooth paste.

quiz.question: How should you run a grinder for these foods?
choices: In short bursts with small batches.
Continuously with the bowl packed full.
Until the bowl feels warm, then add more food.
quiz.because: Small batches and short bursts limit heating and help the grind stay even.

quiz.question: What suggests an uneven grind?
choices: An even powder without whole pieces.
Dust mixed with pieces still left whole.
A paste that holds together when pressed.
quiz.because: Whole pieces among dust show that some food has ground much faster than the rest.

quiz.question: The paste has become too thin after adding liquid. What would you change next time?
choices: Pour all the liquid in before starting.
Keep adding liquid after the paste moves freely.
Add liquid gradually and stop when the blades turn.
quiz.because: Only enough liquid to keep the blades moving is needed; excess turns the paste into soup.

comes_after.why: Spices and nuts are toasted first so that they grind to a finer, more fragrant powder.
